Notes: Earliest documented Jewish settlement: per Josephus (Against Apion 2.44) Ptolemy I Soter sent Jews to 'Cyrene and the other cities of Libya' to strengthen his control of the region. Date given only as the reign of Ptolemy I (304-282 BCE per source); midpoint used (c. 293 BCE). Year Established is based on this settlement. No numbers given.

Jason of Cyrene, Jewish historian whose five-book Greek history of the Maccabean revolt (175-161 BCE) was abridged as 2 Maccabees (2 Macc 2:23); per the Catholic Encyclopedia he wrote 'not long after 160 B.C.' (c. 160 BCE). A Jew of Cyrenean origin; points to a Hellenized Jewish community at Cyrene in the mid-2nd c. BCE. Where he lived when writing is unknown.

1 Maccabees 15:15-23: letter of the Roman consul Lucius, brought by Numenius, telling kings and states not to harm the Jews and sent to a list of places ending 'and Cyprus and Cyrene'. Dated by the context (1 Macc 15:10, year 174 of the Seleucid era = 139/138 BCE), c. 139 BCE. Usually read as a list of places with Jewish communities, so indirect evidence of Jews at Cyrene. No numbers.

Strabo (quoted by Josephus, Ant. 14.7.2 / 14.114-115): at the time of Sulla (c. 85 BCE) the inhabitants of Cyrene were divided into four classes: citizens, farmers, resident aliens and Jews. Lucullus was sent by Sulla to Cyrene to suppress disturbances in which the Jews took a prominent part. Shows a large, separately classed Jewish group in the city; no numbers.

Ephebic list from the gymnasium area of Cyrene (IRCyr C.431, found 1915 SW of the Agora), dated 1st c. BCE to Augustan (100 BCE-14 CE; midpoint used, c. 43 BCE). Includes one name the editors call 'certainly Jewish': Iesous son of Antiphilos (col. 2 line 2). Shows a Jewish youth enrolled in the city's ephebate, i.e. a Hellenized Jewish family with access to the gymnasium. IRCyr EpiDoc file read from the GitHub mirror because the IRCyr site was bot-blocked.

The Greeks of Cyrene harassed the Jews and stopped them sending Temple donations to Jerusalem. Their rights were fully restored only when Augustus and Marcus Agrippa intervened in 14 BCE (Josephus, Ant. 16.160ff.; Agrippa's letter 'to the magistrates, senate, and people of Cyrene', Ant. 16.169-170). Shows an organized community collecting sacred money. No numbers.

Ephebic list from the Agora of Cyrene (IRCyr C.145), dated 3-4 CE by Actian-era year 34. Names identified as Jewish (with reference to Lüderitz's corpus): Ioulios son of Iesous (b.i.40), and Elazar and Agathokles son of Elazar (b.ii.31-32, 'probably Jewish'). Several Jewish ephebes in one list; Applebaum used this to argue that some Jews held full Cyrenean citizenship from Augustus onward.

Mark 15:21: 'Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus', who carried Jesus' cross in Jerusalem (c. 30 CE). A Jew of Cyrenean origin, present in Jerusalem; indirect evidence of the Cyrene community.

Acts 6:9 (c. 34 CE): 'Cyrenians' among the members of a Jerusalem synagogue (with Alexandrians, Cilicians and Asians) who disputed with Stephen. Acts 2:10 also lists Jewish pilgrims from 'the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene' at Pentecost (c. 30 CE). Shows Jews of Cyrenean origin in Jerusalem, enough to share a synagogue there; these are emigrants and pilgrims, not residents of Cyrene.

List of nomophylakes (city law-guardians) of Cyrene (IRCyr C.98, probably from the Nomophylakeion), dated 59-61 CE (Actian years 90-91). Line 8 names Elazar son of Jason, 'presumably a Jew' per the editors. Applebaum suggested descent from the Jason son of Eleazar of 1 Macc 8:17. Evidence of a Jew holding municipal office, cited for Jewish citizenship at Cyrene.

Josephus, War 7.437-450: after the fall of Jerusalem (c. 73 CE) the Sicarius Jonathan, a weaver, led poorer Jews of Cyrene into the desert. The notable Jews of Cyrene informed Catullus, governor of the Libyan Pentapolis. Catullus then had Alexander and his wife Bernice and the wealthy Jews killed, 'no fewer in all than three thousand' (7.445). This is a death toll, ancient figure, not a population count, so Population is left blank. It implies a large and wealthy community with recognized leaders.
